lead: A classifier sees only numbers. Feature engineering turns each document into numbers that separate the classes, and evaluation metrics tell you whether those numbers produced a useful classifier. A spam filter that catches 80 of 90 spam emails but marks 20 good emails as spam faces different costs from one that misses half the spam. Accuracy alone hides this. This chapter covers feature types, feature selection, and the confusion-matrix metrics — precision, recall, F1, macro and micro averages, ROC-AUC — plus cross-validation. These tools are used in spam filtering, support-ticket routing, and review moderation.
prereq: You need: text classifiers from 5.2 and bag-of-words/TF-IDF vectors from 5.1.

blocks.text: A feature is a number computed from a document. The classifier learns a weight for each feature. Good features make the classes separable; a feature with the same value in both classes adds noise.

items: Word n-grams: unigrams such as "refund" and bigrams such as "not good". Bigrams keep negation and short phrases. Vocabulary size grows fast.
Character n-grams: fixed-length character slices. The 3-grams of "refund" are "ref", "efu", "fun", "und". They survive spelling mistakes and work for morphologically rich Indian languages.

TF-IDF weight: tf(t,d) × log(N ÷ df(t)). tf is the count of term t in document d; df is the number of documents containing t; N is the total number of documents. Rare discriminative words get high weight; "the" gets low weight. See 5.1.
Presence flags: 1 if a word or pattern occurs, else 0. A flag for "!!!" or "Rs." or "OTP" can be a strong spam signal.
Document length: token count or number of sentences. Short messages like "call me" differ from long newsletters.
Punctuation and case: count of exclamation marks, ratio of uppercase letters, number of currency symbols.
POS tags: counts of nouns, verbs and adjectives from a tagger (Unit 2). Useful when word identity matters less than syntax.

blocks.text: For a phone SMS spam filter, the feature vector may hold 5,000 word unigrams, 2,000 character 4-grams, a presence flag for "OTP", and the count of digits. Each row is one SMS; each column is one feature.

sections.h3: Feature selection with chi-square and mutual information

blocks.text: A vocabulary of 50,000 words gives 50,000 columns. Most are rare and useless. Feature selection keeps the top k columns that are statistically tied to the class label. Two standard scores are chi-square and mutual information.

blocks.where: O is the observed count in one cell of the 2×2 table (feature present/absent vs class spam/ham); E = (row total × column total) ÷ N; N is the number of training documents. Large χ² means feature and class are not independent.

blocks.text: Mutual information measures how much knowing the feature reduces uncertainty about the class.
I(T;C) = Σ p(t,c) log₂ [ p(t,c) ÷ (p(t) × p(c)) ]
blocks.where: p(t,c) is the fraction of documents with feature value t and class c. I is 0 when feature and class are independent. Keep features with the highest I.

blocks.text: Compute both scores on the training data only. If you select features using the full dataset before cross-validation, the test fold leaks into training and your score is too optimistic. This is a common bug in student projects.
A confusion matrix counts four outcomes for a binary classifier. Take spam as the positive class: TP = spam correctly marked spam; FP = ham marked spam; FN = spam marked ham; TN = ham marked ham.

blocks.where: TP is true positives; FP is false positives. Precision is the fraction of predicted spam that is really spam.
FN is false negatives. Recall is the fraction of real spam that was caught.
P is precision; R is recall. F1 is the harmonic mean and is high only when both P and R are high.
The denominator is the total number of emails. Accuracy is the fraction classified correctly.

blocks.text: Class imbalance makes accuracy misleading. If 91% of emails are ham, a classifier that always says ham gets 91% accuracy and catches zero spam. Always report precision and recall on the rare class. Macro averaging computes the metric per class and takes the unweighted mean; every class counts equally. Micro averaging sums TP, FP and FN over classes first, then computes one metric; large classes dominate.

ROC-AUC plots true positive rate (recall) against false positive rate FP ÷ (FP + TN) as the decision threshold moves. AUC = 0.5 is random; 1.0 is perfect. It is threshold-free but still ignores class balance in the training data. Use stratified k-fold cross-validation: split the data into k folds that keep the same spam/ham ratio, train on k−1 folds, test on the held-out fold, and average the k scores.

figure.caption: The 1000 test emails in four cells. Precision uses the predicted-spam row, 80 of 100; recall uses the actual-spam column, 80 of 90. F1 is 0.842, and accuracy, 970 of 1000, looks better than either.

spec.aria: A two by two confusion matrix with TP 80, FP 20, FN 10 and TN 890, and bars for precision 0.800, recall 0.889, F1 0.842 and accuracy 0.970.

examples.question: A spam classifier is tested on 1000 emails: TP=80, FP=20, FN=10, TN=890. Compute precision, recall, F1 and accuracy.
steps: Total emails = 80 + 20 + 10 + 890 = 1000. Actual spam = TP + FN = 90. Predicted spam = TP + FP = 100.
examples.check:
tp, fp, fn, tn = 80, 20, 10, 890
p = tp / (tp + fp)
r = tp / (tp + fn)
f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r)
acc = (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn)
print(round(p, 3))
print(round(r, 3))
print(round(f1, 3))
print(round(acc, 3))

traps: Accuracy trap: 0.97 looks high, but recall is 0.889 — 10 of 90 spam emails still reach the inbox. On a rare class, report precision and recall, not accuracy.
Precision vs recall swap: precision divides by predicted positives (TP + FP); recall divides by actual positives (TP + FN). Swapping the denominators is the most common exam slip.
Macro vs micro: macro averages class scores equally; micro sums counts first. A 90/10 imbalance makes micro close to accuracy.
Feature-selection leakage: selecting the top chi-square features on all data before cross-validation inflates the score. Select inside each training fold.
Confusion matrix orientation: rows are predicted and columns are actual, or the reverse. Read the labels before computing anything.

quiz.q: Define precision and recall in one sentence each.
quiz.a: Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP), the fraction of predicted positives that are correct. Recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN), the fraction of actual positives that are found.

quiz.q: Why can a classifier with 97% accuracy be useless for spam detection?
quiz.a: If spam is only 9% of emails, a classifier that predicts ham for every email gets about 91% accuracy. It catches zero spam (recall 0), so accuracy hides failure on the rare class.

quiz.q: TP=40, FP=10, FN=20, TN=930. Compute precision, recall and F1.
A team selects the 1,000 best chi-square features using all 10,000 labelled emails, then runs 10-fold cross-validation and reports F1 = 0.95. What is wrong with this result?
quiz.a: Feature selection saw the test folds, so information leaked from test to train. The reported F1 is too optimistic. Feature selection must be redone inside each training fold.

quiz.q: Explain macro and micro averaging when one class is rare.
quiz.a: Macro computes the metric per class and averages the scores equally, so the rare class counts as much as the common one. Micro sums TP, FP and FN over classes first, so the common class dominates. Report which one you used.

quiz.q: A classifier has ROC-AUC = 0.5. What does this mean?
quiz.a: The classifier ranks a random positive no better than a random negative. Its ranking is equivalent to random guessing; changing the threshold cannot fix it.

quiz.q: For Hindi movie reviews typed on phones with spelling variation, would you prefer word unigrams or character n-grams? Why?
quiz.a: Character n-grams are more robust: spelling variants such as "accha" and "acha" share character slices, while word unigrams treat them as different features. Character n-grams also handle suffixes. Word unigrams may still help for frequent correctly spelled words, so combining both is common.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, teams monitor precision at a fixed recall for fraud and spam, because a false negative and a false positive have different costs. Search engines report NDCG and mean average precision, which extend the ranking view beyond ROC-AUC. Calibration checks whether a predicted probability of 0.8 really means 80 out of 100 cases. Search terms: class-imbalance metrics, PR-AUC, stratified cross-validation, feature hashing.
